systems.neoclassical: Stone, symmetry and a restrained bronze. The portfolio as a classical institution.
systems.baroque: Deep shadow, one raking light and gilt on every edge. Composed excess.
systems.aurora: Ribbons of cold light over near-black, and the only world that keeps the three-dimensional diagram.
systems.ethereal: Pastel air, thin serifs and the slowest motion on the site. Almost nothing, precisely placed.
systems.filigree: Fine metalwork on a dark ground. Everything is a drawn line; nothing is a fill.
systems.acanthus: The Corinthian leaf as a digital identity. Straight structure, botanical curves.
systems.anthropomorphic: Rounded, inked and alive. Cards that watch the cursor and buttons with a body.
systems.pixel-art: A sixteen-bit workstation on a four-pixel grid. Stepped motion, hard edges, phosphor green.
systems.conceptual-sketch: Paper, pencil rules and blue-pen marginalia. The thinking, not only the result.
systems.luxury-typography: Black on white and nothing else. The typography is the entire design.
systems.japandi: Paper, clay and one soft cedar. The most space on the site, used as a material rather than left over.
systems.memphis: Sottsass in 1981: shapes with no functional excuse, in flat unmixed colour, around a perfectly sober text block.
systems.bohemian: A room with too many textiles in it, lit at dusk. Nothing has a hard edge; several things have a fringe.
systems.shabby-chic: Chalk paint sanded back at the corners. Every panel is a painted frame whose top coat has come away.
systems.cottagecore: Late afternoon in July, somewhere with no pavement. Wheat, sage and elderflower, held together by a workmanlike serif.
systems.victorian: A study lit by gas: oxblood, walnut and tarnished brass, with every surface occupied on principle.
systems.art-deco: Paris, 1925. Compass and set square only: every curve a struck arc, every ornament one motif stepped down in scale.
systems.art-nouveau: Structure derived from stems. No straight line, no repeated module, and no symmetry a plant would not produce.
systems.mystical-western: The desert at three in the morning: indigo, bone and rust, with a moon and one low fire as the only light.
systems.kitsch: Every decorative layer this site owns, switched on at once — and the body copy still at twelve to one.
systems.y2k: Chrome and frosted plastic, 1999. The only world drawn with a true bevel: light on the top edge, shadow on the bottom.
systems.bauhaus: Three primaries, three forms, one grid. No gradient, no blur, no radius but the true circle.
systems.brutalism: Béton brut: concrete left as the formwork made it, and type at the scale of signage cast into a wall.
systems.cybercore: An interface that shows its own instrumentation. Hairline cyan, monospace throughout, and not one neon blob.
systems.synthwave: Lit entirely from below by the grid and from behind by the sun, so every highlight sits on a bottom edge.
systems.vaporwave: The same decade on a worn tape. Nothing is quite aligned, and the edge on hover is a chromatic split rather than a glow.
systems.pop-art: Lichtenstein rather than Warhol: a keyline, a dot screen for every tone, and four process inks with no fifth.
systems.bento-box: One radius, one border, one accent. The hierarchy is carried by cell size and never by decoration.
systems.graffiti: A wall, not a font. Concrete, pasted panels, and the one soft thing an aerosol can does that a brush cannot.
systems.tenebrism: One source, close and hard, high on one side. Everything it does not reach falls to black rather than to grey.
systems.gothic: The architecture, not the subculture. Every arc meets at an apex, and the page is the tallest on the site.
systems.pointillism: No colour is ever mixed. Two pure hues placed side by side resolve into a third in the eye, and nowhere else.
systems.mixed-media: A combine: photograph, torn newsprint, pencil and brush on one surface, none of them harmonised with the others.
systems.steampunk: The workshop behind the parlour. Everything is fastened, everything reads out, and the ornament would turn if you pushed it.
systems.kawaii: Cute as a proportion system rather than a sticker sheet: two hues, one border weight, and lilac shadows.
systems.coquette: Dressed rather than worn. A hairline trim stitched in from every hem, and the only italic display face on the site.
systems.surrealism: Magritte, not Dalí: the rendering stays sober and only the logic is wrong. Shadows fall where no light could put them.
systems.utilitarian: A measuring instrument. Every mark exists because somebody operating the thing needs it — labels, units, tolerances, a lamp.
systems.mid-century: 1955, and the belief that design was a public good. An elongated pill sitting on a strictly rectilinear grid.
systems.scrapbook: Somebody’s kitchen table: card stock, photo corners, washi tape and a ballpoint caption.
systems.frutiger-aero: 2007: water, glass and sky, and the belief that technology was about to be clean and friendly.
systems.dark-academia: A library at night with one lamp lit, and the longest reading measure on the site. The fantasy is reading.
systems.light-academia: The same library at eleven in the morning. Identical bones, opposite light, and no vignette at all.
systems.wabi-sabi: Asymmetry applied systematically: four different corners on every radius, and no measurement that is a round number.
systems.wild-west: Noon on a wanted poster: heavy slab serif, a double rule around everything, and paper left in a window for a season.
systems.nautical: A chart table below the waterline. One horizontal is privileged over every other line, and the motion is a slow roll about it.
systems.rebus: A CV written as pictures. The puzzle is in the layout rather than in a texture, and the answer is always in red.
systems.glassmorphism: Exactly one glass layer deep, and text never sits on it without an opaque backing. Depth the type does not pay for.
systems.modular-typography: Letters as engineering. A character is not drawn, it is assembled from fixed modules on a fixed pitch.
systems.neo-brutalism: A wireframe that shipped. Saturated flat colour, a black keyline on everything, and a shadow that never blurs.

hero.headline: I build enterprise frontends that hold their shape.
hero.sub: React and TypeScript architecture for regulated financial software — and AI-native workflows that keep the code honest.

about.title: Software that cannot afford to be wrong.
body: I'm a software engineer in Yerevan. I work on financial software — leasing and credit systems where authorization, auditability and correctness aren't features, they're the product.

At Actual Solutions I own the frontend architecture of MK Kredit. It went from an empty repository to roughly fifty business modules covering the complete credit lifecycle: application analysis, credit history, collateral, income and expenses, cash flow, credit committee approval, conclusions, disbursement. I designed its Feature-Sliced architecture, its type-safe authorization model, its centralized API and error-handling layers, and the reusable form and table systems most of the product is built from.

I also work AI-native — as professional practice, not experiment. The interesting problem isn't getting a model to generate code. It's getting generated code to respect architecture, business rules and engineering standards at speed, without eroding the system underneath.
Before engineering I spent two years as a graphic designer. It still shows in how I treat interfaces.

experience.title: Four years, three of them commercial.

actualsolutions.summary: Frontend architecture of MK Kredit, an enterprise leasing and credit management platform.
highlights: Built and evolved a React 19 and TypeScript application from a greenfield codebase into roughly 50 business modules covering the complete leasing lifecycle — application analysis, credit history, collateral, income and expenses, cash flow, credit committee approval, conclusions and disbursement.
Architected the codebase around Feature-Sliced Design with enforced module boundaries and automated CI quality gates, so the application stays navigable as the domain expands.
Designed type-safe authorization, a centralized API layer and a unified error-handling architecture, plus reusable form and data-table systems that most business modules are composed from.
Integrated 36 domain API services spanning 190+ endpoints with JWT authentication and automatic token refresh.
Delivered mobile-first responsive UI, PWA capabilities, a multi-theme design system, user personalization and Armenian-first internationalization.

Applied AI-first and agentic development across requirements, architecture, implementation, refactoring, documentation and code review using Claude Code, specialized agents, project-aware scaffolding and Figma, Jira and Swagger integrations.

Established context engineering, spec-driven development and human-in-the-loop validation so AI-generated code conforms to project architecture, business rules and engineering standards rather than merely compiling.

architecture.title: Fifty modules, one shape.
architecture.lead: Feature-Sliced Design isn't a folder convention. It's a dependency rule: every layer may only reach downward. Enforce that in CI and the fiftieth module costs about what the fifth did.

layers.app: Providers, routing, global configuration. Knows about everything; nothing knows about it.
layers.pages: Route compositions. Assembles widgets — contains no business logic.
layers.widgets: Self-contained blocks: the application table, the credit committee panel.
layers.features: User actions with business meaning: approve, reject, attach collateral.
layers.entities: Domain models — application, client, collateral, payment schedule.
layers.shared: UI kit, API client, hooks, utilities. Knows nothing about the domain.

architecture.closing: Dependencies flow one way. CI fails the build when they don't. That single constraint is what makes fifty modules navigable — and what makes AI-generated code safe to accept.

projects.title: Production work, and public code.
projects.lead: Commercial work is private — it's fintech. The case studies below describe it in the detail I can. The public repositories are architecture studies and challenge builds, and they're labelled as such.

mk-kredit.title: MK Kredit
mk-kredit.shortDescription: Greenfield React 19 and TypeScript frontend for a full enterprise leasing and credit lifecycle: ~50 business modules on Feature-Sliced Design.
mk-kredit.overview: The frontend of a platform banks and leasing organizations run their credit business on: application intake through to disbursement, with the authorization, auditability and workflow rules that regulated lending requires. Built from an empty repository into roughly fifty business modules.
mk-kredit.problem: Leasing and credit operations are long, multi-stage and evidence-heavy. Every application accumulates financial analysis, collateral records, credit history and committee decisions — each stage with different actors, permissions and validation rules. Build this as ordinary screens and it becomes unmaintainable by module fifteen.
mk-kredit.context: Greenfield, regulated domain, Armenian-first user base, an expanding feature surface, and a small team. The architecture had to absorb growth without proportional growth in complexity.
mk-kredit.roleDetail: Frontend architecture and technical direction; the platform systems — authorization, API layer, error handling, forms, tables, theming, internationalization; delivery of lifecycle modules; and establishing the AI-native workflow the team develops with.
mk-kredit.architecture: Feature-Sliced Design, with enforced layer boundaries so dependencies flow one way and business modules stay isolated. On top of it: a centralized Axios client with JWT and automatic token refresh; TanStack Query for all server state; Redux Toolkit for client state; a reusable form system on React Hook Form and Zod; a shared data-table system; a type-safe authorization model; a unified error-handling architecture; a multi-theme design system on Ant Design and SCSS; i18next with Armenian as the primary locale. Automated CI quality gates on GitHub Actions, containerized with Docker, deployed to Azure.
challenges: Keeping fifty business modules navigable — solved by Feature-Sliced layer boundaries enforced in CI rather than by convention.
Integrating 36 domain services across 190+ endpoints without the API layer fragmenting — solved with a single typed client, shared interceptors and centralized error handling.
Modelling permissions for a regulated workflow — solved with a type-safe authorization model, so unauthorized states are unrepresentable rather than merely hidden.
Validation-heavy multi-stage forms — solved with a reusable form system pairing React Hook Form with Zod schemas.
Armenian-first internationalization, including layout and typography for a non-Latin script as the default rather than a retrofit.
Sustaining AI-assisted velocity without architectural erosion — solved with project-aware scaffolding, spec-driven development and human review gates.
results: Greenfield to ~50 business modules covering the full leasing lifecycle.
36 services and 190+ endpoints integrated behind one type-safe, centrally error-handled layer.
Mobile-first responsive UI with PWA capability, multi-theme support and personalization.
Armenian-first internationalization, with CI quality gates in place from the start.
mk-kredit.lessons: Architecture is what makes AI-assisted development safe. Generation speed is only an asset when there are boundaries for generated code to respect — the constraint system is the leverage, not the generator.

ai-native-workflow.title: AI-Native Development Workflow
ai-native-workflow.shortDescription: Agentic development on Claude Code with spec-driven implementation and human review gates — on a regulated fintech codebase.
ai-native-workflow.overview: An internal engineering workflow built on Claude Code, in which AI participates across requirements, architecture, implementation, refactoring, documentation and code review — under constraints that keep its output inside the project's architecture and business rules.
ai-native-workflow.problem: AI-generated code is fast and architecturally indifferent. On a regulated fintech codebase, unconstrained generation produces working code that quietly violates layer boundaries, duplicates existing abstractions and misses domain rules. The cost lands later, as erosion.
ai-native-workflow.roleDetail: Designed the workflow, the context structure and the review gates, then adopted them across the engineering lifecycle.
ai-native-workflow.architecture: Four mechanisms. Context engineering structures the project's architecture, conventions and domain rules as durable context, so generation starts inside the constraints. Project-aware scaffolding generates new modules against the real Feature-Sliced structure rather than generic templates. Spec-driven development puts specification before generation, making the spec the contract. Human-in-the-loop validation adds explicit review gates where an engineer verifies architectural and business-rule compliance before merge. Figma, Jira and Swagger integrations pull design, requirements and API contracts into that context, and specialized agents handle distinct lifecycle jobs rather than one general assistant handling everything.
challenges: Generated code that compiles but violates layer boundaries — caught by scaffolding that starts inside the architecture and CI that enforces it.
Domain rules that a model cannot infer from the codebase alone — solved by encoding them as durable context rather than repeating them per prompt.
Review fatigue at volume — solved by making review gates specific: architectural compliance and business rules, not general code reading.
results: AI-native throughput on a greenfield enterprise codebase, with the architecture holding.
~50 business modules in seven months, inside a Feature-Sliced structure with CI quality gates.
ai-native-workflow.lessons: The interesting problem is not generating code; it is constraining generation. Architecture, specs and review gates are what convert model output into software a bank can run.

fsd-reference.title: Feature-Sliced Design reference build
fsd-reference.shortDescription: React, TypeScript and Vite application structured with Feature-Sliced Design and the React Compiler, used to validate layer boundaries before applying them at enterprise scale.
fsd-reference.overview: A sandbox for the architecture that now underpins a fifty-module fintech platform. Built four months before the role that would depend on it — learning the pattern deliberately, then applying it where it mattered.
fsd-reference.architecture: The six standard Feature-Sliced layers — app, pages, widgets, features, entities, shared — with dependencies permitted only downward, plus the React Compiler enabled to test how the layer structure interacts with automatic memoization.
fsd-reference.lessons: Layer boundaries are cheap to hold from the first commit and expensive to introduce later. Validating that in a sandbox is worth the weekend.
